highlights: Launch design combined voice interaction, connected-home control and remote monitoring
Q-Link app supported remote video streaming and robot control
Manufacturer described automatic charging and Android SDK/App Store support at launch

The native Nano sheet lists 19 kg, maximum 0.8 m/s and four-hour operation versus over ten hours standby. Its 20 Ah/300 W text is retained as an ambiguous electrical label, not converted into Wh or charging duration.

The specification gives 848.32 mm height, 395.22 mm depth and 420.59 mm width, while the August 2017 announcement says 2.7 ft tall. The differing height claims remain visible rather than silently treated as equivalent unit conversions.

Nano uses a 10.1-inch 1080p touch display, cameras, head/arm motion and omnidirectional wheel hardware. Component motion counts are not added into an independently established complete-system DOF value; the 1.5 cm Grade entry is not a slope angle.

The 2017 release announces 2800 USD and planned purchase availability in October, while native pages describe Alexa and Q-Link. These historical claims do not establish an actual first-sale date, current pricing, maintained Android/ROS software, cloud access or current Alexa integration.

Voice interaction, face recognition, video chat and automatic return to charge are manufacturer features. The isolated 98% page text lacks an assigned metric and is not used as recognition accuracy, safety assurance, runtime or measured outcome.

highlights: The native comparison names Professional, Standard and Economic versions. Professional alone lists 75 kg maximum freight; Standard and Economic say None. Freight or attached-equipment capacity is separate from articulated arm lifting.

Professional lists about 18 hours operation and 50 hours standby; Standard about ten hours operation; Economic provides 300 Wh capacity without operating duration. The reception page’s 24/7 language relies on recharging and is not per-charge endurance.

Professional and Standard list powered Mecanum-wheel hardware and 0-5 m/s, while Economic explicitly says push manually and no drive. Generic autonomous mapping, navigation and delivery claims are not copied to the unpowered version.

The performance page’s 20 DOF refers to arms/hands. The version matrix includes head, arm, palm, waist and chassis subcounts; Standard/Economic head detail blocks disagree with their motor-row counts. A complete-system numeric DOF total remains unestablished.

The August 2017 announcement describes a roughly 4.8 ft configuration and 165 lb towing; the January 2018 CES announcement instead gives 4.7 ft, 220 lb, 165 lb attached equipment and 881 lb towing. Dates, load modes and unspecified revisions remain separate; no one figure becomes a universal exact version rating.

The 2017 Max announcement names QIHAN and points to a kingkong.html URL, while the support FAQ uses Sanbot King Kong. This is an identity lead, not explicit proof of identical equipped hardware or a separate new model. First unveiling and the later CES introduction are not confirmed first commercial sale.

highlights: The native product navigation identifies Nano, Elf, Max and Mini ELF. Max has Professional/Standard/Economic columns and Mini ELF has PRO/BASE/RETAIL columns. Software, app, cloud and temperature-screening applications are not additional robot identities.

The 2017 manufacturer release identifies QIHAN Technology for Nano and Elf. The native Brand Story says Sanbot robots are manufactured by Sanbot Innovation; both catalog manufacturer labels share the Sanbot product-brand profile without asserting a verified legal rename or company merger.

Nano and Elf runtime, standby and charging hardware remain separate. Nano height differs between the announcement and specification; Elf robot mass/dimensions are not overwritten by the charging-pile section or erroneous secondary-unit suffix.

Max Professional freight, 18-hour endurance and powered navigation do not apply universally to Standard or manually pushed Economic. Arm/hand DOF, head-count inconsistencies, energy labels and 24/7 recharge-enabled service do not become complete-system performance ratings.

Mini ELF privacy switches and 3D sensing depend on variant. Its AC input, shared articulated face/neck and pose envelopes do not establish a mobile humanoid or battery rating. Auxiliary infrared screening is explicitly not medical detection.

The historical Max announcement links to kingkong.html while the support page says King Kong; exact equipped identity remains unproven. Xiaohai 2.0 is a named customized customs configuration. The unversioned 2015 Sanbot account does not establish a separate distinct model, and Donkey is only named as a proprietary solution. The retained 2016-2018 copyright, historical apps/partners and warranty text do not prove current production, ongoing cloud services, maintained Android/ROS software, independent outcomes, exclusive USPs or market leadership.
